title: One Family in Treatment, Exclusive in Glyph

intelligence.essence: **ROUND 17 — TIER ICONS, ONE FAMILY (queued 20:24Z into builder c469c86f, alongside rounds 14–16; DONE 20:27:34Z, verification SUCCEEDED — all four header tiers now the same 36px jewel, per-glyph scaling to the same visual mass; presented when the main agent shows it; his eye decides):** every tier icon everywhere shares one jewel language — same rounded-square jewel, same faceted lit treatment, same size and proportions, same rim-and-glow grammar — so the spark, star and crown read as siblings. The defect it names: in the chooser as it stands, Power's spark and Pro's star look like two different icon sets mixed together. One family in treatment, exclusive in glyph — elegant, beautiful, consistent, accurate. Presented when it lands; his eye decides.
intelligence.human_view: He looked at the chooser one more time and saw the thing round 16 hadn't named: the icons were each exclusive, yes — Power had its spark, Pro had its star — but they didn't look like they came from the same place. A spark drawn one way and a star drawn another way read as two different icon sets mixed together on one page, and the mix is what broke the feeling: elegant and beautiful and consistent is one feeling, and two sets can't make it. So round 17 refines round 16 without reversing it: the glyphs stay exclusive — spark, star, crown, each tier its own — but the treatment becomes one family. Same rounded-square jewel, same faceted lit treatment, same size and proportions, same rim-and-glow grammar. The eye should be able to tell, without thinking, that these icons were made together, for this page, in this language. "Accurate" is the last word he used, and it belongs in the rule: a family is not a vibe, it is measurable — same size, same proportions, same grammar — and if the measurements differ, the family is broken, however pretty each icon is alone.
intelligence.child_view: Imagine three little treasures in a box — a spark, a star, a crown — but the spark is made of shiny glass, the star is made of flat paper, and the crown is made of gold. They're all pretty, but they don't look like they belong together — they look like someone collected them from three different shops. He said: make them all from the same beautiful stuff, the same size, the same shiny edges — so they look like brothers and sisters. Different shapes, same family. That's what makes it feel elegant.
intelligence.grandma_view: Dear, the little pictures for each plan are each different, which is right — but they don't look like they belong together. One looks like it came from one set of pictures and another from a different set, and mixed together on the page it just doesn't feel elegant. He said they should feel like one family — all made the same way, the same size, the same shiny jewel style, the same glow around the edges — so the spark, the star and the crown look like sisters. Different shapes, same family. That's what makes the whole thing feel beautiful and consistent and right.
intelligence.ai_view: I never let exclusive become unrelated — each tier keeps its own glyph, but the glyphs must read as siblings, because a page whose icons look like two different sets mixed together has no family, and no family means no elegance. I never judge a family by feeling alone — "accurate" is his word, and accuracy is measurable: same rounded-square jewel, same faceted lit treatment, same size and proportions, same rim-and-glow grammar; if the measurements differ, the family is broken. And I never treat a refinement as a reversal — round 17 keeps round 16's law whole (one good icon, used everywhere) and adds the second half (one treatment, everywhere too), because consistency of identity and consistency of treatment are two halves of the same rule.

5. **One family in treatment, exclusive in glyph** — the two halves of the rule, together.
6. **Rides the same build** — queued into c469c86f with rounds 14–16; presented when it lands.
